title: Adolescent screen use is a negotiated household and platform-governance problem, not only an individual time problem
source_unit: European Commission Flash Eurobarometer 579, Impact of excessive screen time and social media on young people’s mental health
geography: European Union, all 27 Member States; adolescents aged 13–18 and their parents

observations.period: 30 March–16 April 2026; ordinary school-day and weekend screen use

denominator.unit: EU adolescents aged 13–18 interviewed across all 27 Member States

school_day_high_use.unit: percent reporting more than 6 hours of screen time on a typical school day

weekend_high_use.unit: percent reporting more than 6 hours of screen time on a typical weekend day

weekend_extreme_use.unit: percent reporting more than 10 hours of screen time on a typical weekend day

parent_teen_gap.value: Adolescents reported 4.5 hours online on school days and 6.1 hours on weekend days, while parents estimated 3.4 and 5.3 hours respectively

observations.method: EU-wide Flash Eurobarometer survey interviewing adolescents and a separate parent sample, with country-comparable weighted results.
observations.uncertainty: Screen-time measures are self-reported or parent-estimated and do not establish device-level exposure, platform-specific use, clinical impairment, or causal effects.
observations.subgroup: Adolescents aged 13–18, parents, school-day versus weekend users, and respondents across all EU Member States.
observations.counterinterpretation: High online time can include connection, learning, creativity, and social support; duration alone is an imprecise proxy for harm or wellbeing.

observations.period: 2026; social-media entry age, emotional experience, and activity displacement

denominator.unit: EU adolescents aged 13–18 in the youth survey

early_entry_gradient.value: Those starting social media before age 10 reported 7.5 hours of weekend screen time versus 5.7 hours among those starting after age 14
early_entry_gradient.unit: reported average hours per weekend day by age-of-entry group

social_distress.value: Nearly 1 in 3 adolescents reported feeling stressed, sad, or socially excluded because of social media

comparison_pressure.unit: percent reporting comparing themselves with others on social media

activity_displacement.value: Reported screen-related difficulties included concentration problems, tiredness, and reduced time for hobbies and other activities

observations.method: Cross-sectional youth survey with self-reported age of social-media initiation, current use, experiences, and perceived symptoms.
observations.uncertainty: The age-of-entry gradient is observational and may reflect prior vulnerability, family context, platform choice, socioeconomic conditions, or recall; it is not a causal estimate of early entry.
observations.subgroup: Adolescents with different social-media entry ages, gender and age groups, and differing exposure to offline activities and support.
observations.counterinterpretation: Earlier entry may be a marker of broader digital access or social circumstances rather than the cause of later screen time or distress; online connection can also offset isolation.

observations.period: 2026; harmful content, mental-health support, and household policy demand

denominator.unit: EU adolescents aged 13–18, with 12750 parents interviewed separately

problematic_content.unit: percent of adolescents reporting encountering problematic online content, including hate speech, body pressure, violence, or misinformation

mental_health_support.unit: percent of adolescents requesting better access to mental-health support

parent_harm_perception.unit: percent of parents saying social media harms their child’s mental wellbeing

restriction_support.unit: percent of parents supporting additional age limits or restrictions on social-media use

governance_route.value: Adolescents and parents place the problem across platform design, harmful content, household guidance, age rules, and access to support rather than screen duration alone

observations.method: Paired adolescent and parent survey frames covering use, symptoms, harmful experiences, perceived impacts, support needs, and policy preferences.
observations.uncertainty: Reported exposure and perceived harm are not verified incidents or clinical diagnoses; parent and adolescent responses are not linked at the individual household level in the published summary.
observations.subgroup: Adolescents, parents, families, schools, mental-health services, platforms, regulators, and young people encountering harmful or misleading content.
observations.counterinterpretation: Restrictions may reduce some exposures but can also shift risk to less visible channels, limit beneficial connection, or create privacy and enforcement burdens; the survey does not compare interventions.

related_sources.claim: European Commission summary of the survey’s headline findings and child-safety policy context.
Commission public-health guidance connecting screen use, platform design, family support, and mental-health protection.

boundary: This record adds a large cross-national paired survey on adolescent screen use, social-media experience, harmful content, parent perception, and support demand. It does not establish that screen duration causes mental illness, identify platform-level causal effects, validate parent–teen discrepancies as measurement error, or evaluate age limits, design changes, or mental-health interventions.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: EU data catalogue and European Commission materials reviewed for field dates, paired sample sizes, screen-time distributions, parent–teen estimates, age-of-entry comparison, distress, content exposure, support demand, and restriction preferences.
